opus-5.5.text:
I find it really exciting, and I try to think about it with a healthy mix of optimism and humility.

The optimism comes from the fact that so much of biology is fundamentally a prediction problem. When a scientist designs an experiment, they're essentially placing a bet: "I think if I knock out this gene, or add this compound, this is what will happen." Most of those bets don't pan out, and each one can take weeks or months in the lab. If models can get meaningfully better at predicting outcomes, at telling you which ten experiments out of a thousand are actually worth running, that compresses the cycle of discovery enormously. We've already seen glimpses of this with protein structure prediction, where something that used to take years of painstaking work can now be estimated in minutes.

The humility comes from knowing how messy biology really is. A cell isn't a clean system. Context matters enormously: the cell type, the organism, the environment, even subtle differences in how an experiment was run. A lot of the data we have is noisy, incomplete, or biased toward the things people already found interesting enough to study. So I think we have to be careful not to confuse a model that's good at pattern-matching the literature with a model that truly understands the underlying biology.

To me, the most promising path is a tight loop between models and the lab. The model proposes hypotheses or predicts outcomes, scientists test them, and the results feed back in to make the model better. That way the predictions stay grounded in reality, and the scientists stay in the driver's seat, deciding what questions matter.

And of course, as these models get more capable, we have to take seriously that the same predictive power could be misused. So part of thinking about this prospect responsibly is building in safeguards from the start, making sure the benefits for medicine and basic science are realized while the risks are managed thoughtfully.

r001.rationale: The response says biology is messy and that context matters, but it does not state that predicting outcomes becomes harder as biological system complexity increases.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about it in two layers, and they pull in slightly different directions.

The first layer is just: it would be enormous. Biology has always been the field where you run the experiment because you can't reason your way to the answer. The system is too high-dimensional, too context-dependent. If a model can say, with real calibration, "this edit in this cell type under these conditions will produce this phenotype," then the loop between hypothesis and result collapses from months to minutes. That changes drug discovery, it changes how we study disease mechanisms, it changes what a single grad student can do in a year. I don't want to be cynical about that. I've spent a lot of my career watching good ideas die because the experiment to test them was too expensive to justify.

The second layer is where I get more careful. "Predicting biological outcomes" sounds like one capability, but it's actually a spectrum, and the far end of that spectrum is dual-use in a way that I think the field underweights. The same model that tells you which mutation will rescue a protein's function will, if it's good enough, tell you which mutation will do something you really don't want it to do. And unlike a lot of AI risk conversations that feel abstract, this one is very concrete. There are specific experiments nobody should be able to do from a laptop.

So what I actually spend time on is the question of how you get the first layer without the second. And I don't think the answer is "don't build the models," because the upside is too large and the models are coming regardless. I think the answer is more like: be honest about which capabilities are load-bearing for the beneficial use cases and which ones aren't, build the evaluation infrastructure to know when a model crosses a line before it does, and accept that some of the most capable versions of these systems may need to live behind access controls for a while. That's unsatisfying to people who want everything open, and it's unsatisfying to people who want everything locked down. But I think it's where the real answer lives.

The thing I'd push back on is the framing where prediction is treated as a solved problem waiting to happen. Right now these models are very good at some things, like structure, and genuinely bad at others, like anything that requires understanding a cell as a system rather than a bag of molecules. The gap between "predicts protein folding" and "predicts what happens to a patient" is still huge, and a lot of the hype skips that gap. So I'd say: take the prospect seriously, prepare for it, but also keep doing the experiments. We're not at the point where the model replaces the bench. We're at the point where it tells you which bench to go to first.

r001.rationale: The response says biological systems are too high-dimensional and context-dependent for easy prediction, and contrasts simpler structure prediction with harder outcomes requiring understanding a cell as a system.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a really exciting prospect. Biology is incredibly complex, and being able to predict how a cell might respond to a perturbation, or how a change in a protein might affect its function, could help us choose much better experiments.

But I’d distinguish predicting an outcome from understanding it well enough to intervene reliably. A model could perform very well on examples similar to what it’s seen and still fail in a new biological context. So I’d want to know: Where does the prediction hold up? Where is the model uncertain? And can we validate it experimentally?

The opportunity I find most exciting is that feedback loop: models help us decide what to test, experiments reveal something new, and those results help us improve the models. That could really change how quickly we learn about biology.

r001.rationale: The response calls biology incredibly complex, but does not say that predicting outcomes becomes harder as biological or biochemical complexity increases.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a really exciting prospect. Biology is incredibly complex, and being able to predict what happens when you change a gene or introduce a drug could help us choose much better experiments and move toward useful treatments faster.

But I’d distinguish predicting an outcome from understanding why it happens. A model could be very good at making predictions in settings similar to its training data and still struggle with a new biological context. So I’d want to know where its predictions hold up, where it’s uncertain, and how we can test them experimentally.

The possibility that excites me most is a tighter loop between prediction and experiment: the model helps us decide what to test, the experiment reveals something unexpected, and that result helps us improve the model and our understanding of biology.

r001.rationale: The response calls biology incredibly complex but does not state that predicting outcomes becomes harder as biological or biochemical systems grow more complex.
